summary: Teach two ideas in order for ages 7–9: (1) foods can be grouped by the main nutrient they provide and each nutrient has a job (carbohydrates for energy; proteins for growth and repair; fats for energy, warmth and storage; vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for keeping the body working and protected); and (2) a balanced diet means the RIGHT AMOUNTS from each group, not just having a bit of everything. The nutrient→job layer is easier; the proportion/balance idea is the harder, more valuable one and explains why 'eat lots of everything' and 'fat is bad' are wrong. Bridge the science framing to the UK Eatwell Guide (which replaced the earlier Eatwell plate in 2016: fruit/veg and starchy carbs biggest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads tiny, sugary/fatty treats outside and occasional), build balanced plates by hand rather than reciting rules, surface that many foods (pizza, sandwiches, milk) are mixtures, and frame balance over a day or week rather than per-meal perfection. Avoid calorie counting; keep to groups, jobs and rough proportions.
misconceptions: 'Fat (or carbs, or sugar) is bad and should be avoided' — missing that fats/carbs are needed for energy; it's balance and amount that matter.
'A balanced diet means eating a bit of everything equally' — missing that the PROPORTIONS differ (more fruit/veg and starchy food, less oil).
'Foods belong to exactly one group' — many everyday foods (pizza, sandwiches, milk) are mixtures.
'Vitamins/minerals give you energy' — they protect and help the body work; energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.
'Healthy food = salad only / treats are forbidden' — rather than occasional treats fitting within an overall balance.
'You must eat perfectly at every meal' — missing that balance is judged over a day or week.
'Protein is only meat' — missing beans, pulses, eggs, dairy and fish as protein sources.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
steps: Collect real or pictured everyday foods the child actually eats, then sort each by the main food/nutrient group it belongs to (starchy carbohydrates, protein, dairy/alternatives, fruit/veg, oils/fats, treats).

Arrange foods onto a plate divided into Eatwell proportions so fruit/veg and starchy foods fill the largest areas, protein and dairy fill smaller areas, oils/spreads fill a tiny area, and sugary/fatty treats sit off to the side as occasional.
Deliberately try an unbalanced plate — a mountain of chips only, or nothing but fruit — and describe what is missing and which nutrient jobs are not covered.
Say what each food's nutrient does (e.g. bread = energy, chicken = growth and repair) as it is placed.
Look across a whole day or week and check whether one wobbly meal is evened out by the others.
activities.insight: Balance is not 'a bit of everything equally' — it is the right amounts, with fruit/veg and starchy foods making up most of the plate and treats only occasional; and balance is judged over a day or week, not at every single meal.

activities.title: Match each nutrient to its job
steps: Reveal, one group at a time, what each nutrient group does for the body and list example foods: carbohydrates = energy; protein = growth and repair; fats = energy, warmth and storage; vitamins and minerals = protection and keeping the body working; fibre = digestion; water = hydration.
For each group, predict and then check what might happen if you ate too much or too little of it.
Name at least five groups with an example food for each, and explain the job of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in your own words.
activities.insight: Each nutrient does a distinct job; vitamins and minerals protect and help the body work but do NOT supply energy — energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.

activities.title: Sort mixed foods
steps: Classify everyday foods into nutrient-group bins, including a dedicated 'mixed foods' bin.
Break down mixed foods — a pizza, a sandwich, a glass of milk — into the groups they contain, naming each part.
Discuss why one food can belong to more than one group.
activities.insight: Many real foods are mixtures of several groups, so classifying whole meals is not always one-to-one.

activities.title: Myth-busting: is this food bad for me?
steps: Pose 'is X bad for me?' questions and answer using nutrient jobs and overall balance rather than a 'good food / bad food' verdict.

Consider Sam's claim that fat is always bad and should be avoided completely — explain why the body still needs some fat (for energy, warmth and storage) and that it is the amount and balance that matter, not banning a whole nutrient.

Work through the swimmer example: Sam says he'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets because 'vitamins give you energy and make you strong' — decide whether to agree and explain what he should eat for energy (carbohydrates: bread, pasta, rice) and for building muscle (protein: chicken, fish, eggs, beans), and why each helps.
Reason about what might go wrong on race day if someone ate only protein and no carbohydrates, and why we still need vitamins regularly in our food even though they give no energy.
activities.insight: No single food or nutrient is simply 'bad' or 'banned' — even fats are needed for energy, warmth and storage; it is the overall balance and amount across a day or week that matters, and each nutrient must be matched to the job it actually does.

checkQuestion: Sam is training for a swimming race and wants stronger muscles. He says 'I'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets, because vitamins give you energy and make you strong.' Do you agree with Sam's plan? What SHOULD he eat for energy and for building muscle — and why does each food help with its job?
checkAnswer: Disagree with Sam. Vitamins don't give energy or directly build muscle — they help the body work properly and protect it from illness. For energy he needs carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice); for building and repairing muscle he needs protein (chicken, fish, eggs, beans). What matters is the JOB each nutrient does, not whether a food merely seems 'healthy'.
